header:
Date: 2025-11-10
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Priya Raman (Redwood AE), Marcus Lin (Redwood SE), Ellen Park (CTO, Nova Payments), Rahul Mehta (Platform Eng), Sofia Gomes (SecOps)
Recording: cloud-recording-2025-11-10-1400.mp4
summary: Weekly POC sync to review dedicated sizing numbers, autoscaling policies and burst behavior. Agreed to run a 500-concurrent burst test in staging; Redwood to send updated sizing and pricing; customer to share real QPS distribution and compliance items. Discussed tradeoffs between pre-provisioned capacity and burstable autoscaling, KV/prefix caching to reduce tokens and cost, and fallback model variants for graceful degradation.
transcript:
[00:00] Priya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to 45 min, quick roll call?
[00:06] Ellen: hi, Ellen here, rahul and sofi are with me but rahul will drive the traffic numbers.
[00:12] Rahul: hey all, Rahul on the platform eng team.
[00:16] Sofia: Sofia, secops.
[00:19] Marcus: Marcus from Redwood SE, thanks for having us.
[00:23] Priya: quick agenda, sizing review, autoscaling policy decisions (cooldowns, burst), runbook for overload, and next steps.
[01:02] Ellen: sounds good, last week you sent the initial t-shirt sizes, we looked at them, a couple questions: the p95 looked optimistic for peak.
[01:18] Marcus: yeah that's expected, the first pass assumed average seq lengths from your sample, but if you're bursty we should add headroom or allow burst capacity. we can do either reserved + burst or fully autoscale with warm pools.
[01:36] Rahul: we are seeing sustained 80 qps during business hours and spikes to ~420 qps for 2-3 minutes after batch jobs, plus some ad-hoc traffic hitting 500 occasionally.
[01:50] Priya: okay that helps. for Dedicated we'd recommend baseline reserved capacity sized for your 95th sustained, plus a burst buffer — we can define burst as either pre-warmed instances or ephemeral autoscale to x more GPUs.
[02:12] Ellen: cost is a concern, so what's the tradeoff between keeping warm GPUs vs paying for ephemeral bursts?
[02:20] Marcus: warm GPUs cost but give lower cold-start latency. ephemeral autoscale has a cold start penalty depending on region and model — often 20-40s to get GPU-backed nodes ready unless we use warm-pools. also batching behavior changes with scale.
[02:38] Rahul: can we set different cooldowns? like shorter scale-up fast, but slower scale-down?
[02:45] Marcus: yes, that's what we typically suggest: aggressive scale-up (30s–1m) with conservative scale-down (10–15m) to avoid flapping. you can also set maximum burst concurrency and a per-route fallback to a smaller model variant.
[03:05] Sofia: on fallback models, from a secops perspective we need to ensure degraded responses still meet our compliance for PII handling — how does Redwood ensure log scrubbing on a fallback?
[03:18] Marcus: we have request-level routing policies; fallback models keep the same data handling pipeline — logs follow the same retention rules and KMS encryption; I'll share the devops-security appendix. arch note though: some smaller model variants might not support the same plugins — we'll list which ones do.
[03:40] Ellen: perfect, please send that.
[04:02] Priya: quick dive into numbers — Marcus, can you walk through the sizing table?
[04:10] Marcus: sure, slide data: for model redwood-compat-7b-qat (we're using as reference) — baseline: 4x A10-equivalent per 100 qps for p95 < 200ms with batching. that scales roughly linearly. for your 80 sustained we suggested 4 GPUs baseline. for spikes to 500 we recommend burst capacity to add +12 GPUs ephemeral (so total 16). that's the conservative plan, cheaper option is to pack more batch size and accept higher p95.
[04:48] Rahul: those A10 numbers feel high? our seq len distribution is short — median 64 tokens, 95th 280 tokens.
[04:55] Marcus: short seq helps, yeah. if your effective seq length median is 64, we probably can shave ~20% off those numbers. but tail behavior (280) increases KV cache pressure and per-token compute.
[05:12] Ellen: what's the KV cache strategy to reduce cost?
[05:18] Marcus: two levers: prefix caching and request-level KV reuse. prefix caching caches common initial tokens (like system prompts) at route level. second is cross-request KV reuse for sessions to avoid recomputing context. That reduces tokens sent to the model and lowers compute. we'll propose a caching config — for POC we recommend a 24-hour session cache and route-level prompt cache.
[05:44] Priya: note — configuring prefix caching reduces burst GPU needs because requests are shorter on average.
[05:50] Rahul: good, we'll try to provide a sample of typical prompts.
[06:02] Ellen: another question: what about quantization? can we use int8 or q4 to lower footprint?
[06:08] Marcus: yes, quantization helps. we can run a quantized variant in Dedicated; tradeoffs are throughput vs slight potential quality delta. for inference-critical flows we keep FP16 or q8. we can recommend quantization profiles per route.
[06:30] Rahul: can Redwood do autoscaling tied to different metrics? like GPU utilization vs request queue length?
[06:36] Marcus: yes, both. we typically use a hybrid: scale on queued requests and p95 latency, and have GPU util thresholds as backstop. queue-based scaling reacts to sudden bursts better.
[06:52] Priya: want to discuss cooldowns and burst caps concretely — propose: scale-up policy: queue > 20 triggers +2 instances up to burst cap, scale-down: idle < 2 for 10 minutes then remove. burst cap at +12 GPUs. does that sound reasonable?
[07:10] Rahul: yes, but we need to make sure our SLA is preserved; what is Redwood's SLA for Dedicated?
[07:18] Priya: for Dedicated we offer uptime SLA and latency targets per plan — I'll include the exact SLA text in the follow-up. typically we guarantee 99.9% for availability.
[07:28] Sofia: on logs and audit — what's retention? we need 13 months for certain events.
[07:34] Marcus: default retention is 90 days; extended retention is an add-on — we can support 13 months for audit logs, and logs are encrypted with your KMS. Sofia, I'll send the retention pricing and the KMS integration doc.
[07:48] Ellen: ok. about the burst test — how should we run it?
[07:52] Marcus: recommended: run a staged ramp test in your staging env emulating 500 concurrent short-seq requests for 5 minutes, then sustain 420 qps for 3 minutes, observe p95/p99, GPU util, queue length, and cold start time. Redwood can help orchestrate the test or provide a harness.
[08:12] Rahul: we prefer Redwood to run it with your harness to avoid environmental differences.
[08:16] Marcus: we can do that. we'll need a staging endpoint and sample prompt sets.
[08:22] Priya: action item: Rahul to share sample prompts and a staging endpoint by 11/12. Marcus to run burst test by 11/14. Priya to send sizing + pricing by 11/12.
[08:36] Ellen: good. one other topic: cost model for sustained vs burst — can you show cost per token and per-hour GPU for both options?
[08:45] Priya: yes, the updated spreadsheet will include per-token math, committed discount options and burst rates.
[08:50] Rahul: what about network egress and cross-region failover behavior?
[08:55] Marcus: cross-region failover is supported; egress costs depend on cloud region and are passed through. for critical workloads we recommend co-locating in your primary region and enabling multi-region standby for DR.
[09:08] Sofia: security question — if a fallback model variant is used, are logs separated or mixed? we need strict separation for certain data flows.
[09:16] Marcus: logs are tagged by route and model variant; retention and access controls are per-route. we can create separate log buckets per model if that helps your segmentation.
[09:27] Ellen: that works.
[09:35] Priya: quick note about batching — bigger batch sizes improve throughput but increase tail latency. with your short median seq we can be aggressive on batching for background flows. for interactive flows keep small batch sizes.
[09:52] Rahul: makes sense. for interactive UI we need p95 < 500ms ideally.
[09:58] Marcus: with 4 GPUs baseline and small batches we should hit that for typical prompts; under heavy spike we might see degrade to ~1s unless burst capacity is warmed.
[10:14] Ellen: can Redwood guarantee warm-pool size?
[10:18] Priya: yes, warm-pools are part of Dedicated config — you can reserve N warm nodes and pay a lower warm-pool rate versus full GPU rate; that'll cut cold start at the cost of some baseline.
[10:30] Rahul: how about prewarming with container snapshots to cut start time?
[10:34] Marcus: we use image snapshots and warm caches; with warm-pools cold start can be <10s typically. without warm-pools it's higher.
[10:45] Sofia: any compliance concern with warm-pools? like data lingering in GPU memory?
[10:50] Marcus: we zero GPU memory between sessions and clear KV cache on teardown; we also use per-request encryption and ephemeral storage for any temp assets. I'll add those details to the security appendix.
[11:06] Priya: moving to runbook for overload — suggestion: overflow to smaller model with degraded features + circuit breaker that returns 429 after X failures and notifies on-call.
[11:18] Rahul: ok, can we tune the circuit breaker threshold? we want to avoid 429s during short spikes.
[11:23] Marcus: absolutely, threshold and backoff are configurable. recommended pattern: retry with exponential backoff and let autoscaler add capacity; if queue > 200 for > 2 minutes then degrade.
[11:36] Ellen: we'll want observability — token-level cost per route, p95/p99 dashboards.
[11:42] Priya: Redwood console includes token-level cost, per-route latency, traces and a rollout dashboard. we'll share screenshots and access for your team to preview.
[11:52] Rahul: ok let's confirm who will have admin access.
[11:55] Sofia: SecOps needs admin for logs and key rotation.
[11:59] Priya: noted. we'll include roles and suggested RBAC mappings in the follow-up.
[12:10] Marcus: quick note on the model variants supported for fallback — I'll add a table of which quantized variants include plugin support.
[12:18] Ellen: great. any open risks?
[12:22] Priya: risk list: potential cost blowout on burst if warm-pools insufficient, fallbacks may lack plugins, and extended log retention adds cost. we'll surface mitigations in the follow-up.
[12:34] Rahul: that covers it. next steps recap?
[12:38] Priya: recap — Priya send sizing/pricing + SLA text + RBAC suggestions by 11/12; Marcus run burst test by 11/14 and send logs; Rahul provide sample prompts and staging endpoint by 11/12; Sofia confirm retention and compliance items by 11/13.
[12:58] Ellen: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[13:00] Priya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the spreadsheet and security docs.
[44:30] (end)
